metric.debugger_profiler_support.candidate_universe: Preserved candidate universe and findings from certified legacy work unit ecosystem-tooling--part-2--rust; recertification did not select a new language-specific target.

component_findings.advanced_debug: Preserved paid evidence (ecosystem-tooling--part-2--rust): Rust has solid, mainstream native-debugger coverage (GDB/LLDB with rustc DWARF info, rust-gdb/rust-lldb wrappers, a maintained LLDB fork) and good IDE integration (VS Code+CodeLLDB, RustRover's bundled visual debugger). The profiler ecosystem is mature and cross-platform (perf/cargo-flamegraph, samply, Valgrind/Cachegrind/Callgrind/DHAT, heaptrack, tokio-console for async). However, the Rust compiler team's own 2026 debugging survey explicitly states debugging remains one of the most-cited developer pain points, with named unresolved gaps in async debugging, expression evaluation, and cross-debugger/version consistency, which caps this below top-tier scores reserved for languages without suc
component_findings.basic_debug: Preserved paid evidence (ecosystem-tooling--part-2--rust): IDE integration is mainstream and multi-vendor: VS Code integration via CodeLLDB: "<cite index="12-7">VS Code with the rust-analyzer extension and CodeLLDB offers breakpoints, variable inspection, and watch expressions without leaving your editor.</cite>" and a 2026 guide lists it as a required companion extension: "<cite index="7-5">Key extensions: rust-analyzer (required), CodeLLDB (debugging), crates (dependency management), Even Better TOML (Cargo.toml editing), Error Lens (inline errors).</cite>"
component_findings.cpu_profile: Preserved paid evidence (ecosystem-tooling--part-2--rust): cargo-flamegraph is a de facto standard, one-command CPU profiler wrapper: "<cite index="25-9,25-10,25-11">The community convention is to use the cargo-flamegraph crate. It wraps the perf commands and handles the stackcollapse scripts for you. Running cargo flamegraph is the standard way to get a graph in seconds.</cite>" and it is cross-platform: "<cite index="21-2,21-3">flamegraph is a Cargo command that uses perf/DTrace to profile your code and then displays the results in a flame graph. It works on Linux and all platforms that support DTrace (macOS, FreeBSD, NetBSD, and possibly Windows).</cite>"
component_findings.integration_platforms: Preserved paid evidence (ecosystem-tooling--part-2--rust): Rust has solid, mainstream native-debugger coverage (GDB/LLDB with rustc DWARF info, rust-gdb/rust-lldb wrappers, a maintained LLDB fork) and good IDE integration (VS Code+CodeLLDB, RustRover's bundled visual debugger). The profiler ecosystem is mature and cross-platform (perf/cargo-flamegraph, samply, Valgrind/Cachegrind/Callgrind/DHAT, heaptrack, tokio-console for async). However, the Rust compiler team's own 2026 debugging survey explicitly states debugging remains one of the most-cited developer pain points, with named unresolved gaps in async debugging, expression evaluation, and cross-debugger/version consistency, which caps this below top-tier scores reserved for languages without suc
component_findings.memory_profile: Preserved paid evidence (ecosystem-tooling--part-2--rust): Memory profiling has dedicated first-party-adjacent tooling: "<cite index="23-7,23-8">Memory profiling in Rust has also evolved, with tools like heaptrack and DHAT (Dynamic Heap Allocation Tool) providing detailed insights into heap allocations. Heaptrack, available on Linux, tracks memory usage and helps identify allocation hotspots, while DHAT, part of Valgrind, offers dynamic heap profiling to detect memory leaks and allocation patterns.</cite>" plus an async-specific diagnostic tool: "<cite index="26-9">Use tokio-console when debugging async applications that stall on channel backpressure or lock contention.</cite>"

component_findings.breadth_maintenance: Preserved paid evidence (ecosystem-tooling--part-2--rust): Rust has an official, org-backed, actively-maintained LSP (rust-analyzer) with broad multi-editor reach (VS Code, JetBrains via RustRover/IntelliJ plugin, Neovim, Emacs, Helix, Zed) plus a dedicated commercial full-IDE (RustRover) layering deep refactoring/navigation on top. This is close to best-in-class breadth and maturity; points are withheld only for acknowledged rough edges in macro-expansion tooling and general feature completeness relative to a hypothetical perfect score.
